term: "False Positive"

## Simple explanation

A false positive occurs when a model predicts that a condition is present
even though it is actually absent. For example, an email filter may label
a legitimate message as spam.

## Technical explanation

In binary classification, a false positive (FP) is an instance with a
negative actual label and a positive predicted label. The false-positive
rate is $FP/(FP+TN)$, while precision is $TP/(TP+FP)$. These metrics
answer different questions and depend on the chosen decision threshold.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

False positives can create unnecessary reviews, block legitimate users,
or cause harmful interventions. Their acceptable rate depends on the
application and must be considered alongside false negatives.

## How it works

The model produces a score and a decision rule assigns the positive
label when the score meets a threshold. A negative example above that
threshold becomes a false positive. Changing the threshold can alter
the balance between false positives and false negatives.

## Practical example

For a penguin-versus-ostrich classifier where ostrich is the positive
class, a penguin image predicted as ostrich is a false positive.

## Common misconceptions

- A false positive is not the same as a false-negative error.
- A lower false-positive rate may come at the cost of more false
  negatives.
- The term only has meaning relative to a defined positive class and
  reference label.
